title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Pittsfield Township tightens zoning rules amid statewide pushback on power and water demands.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Today we're starting with Pittsfield Township drafting zoning changes aimed at data centers after residents raised alarms over noise, traffic and power demand.
That sounds like a big step for a township right next to Ann Arbor. What's driving this move right now?
Residents have been vocal about how these facilities could strain the local grid and push up utility rates for everyone if safeguards aren't in place.
How does this fit into what's been happening across the state lately?
It's part of a pattern where communities are stepping in to set their own rules before projects get too far along.
What kind of history are we looking at here with these fights?

Local governments have been weighing whether they can block projects that pull massive power and water loads, and yesterday Monroe Township asked a federal judge to toss a $300 million lawsuit from a developer after it banned new facilities.
That case sounds like it could set a precedent either way. Who are the main players involved?

You've got townships trying to protect residents, developers pushing for the economic upside, and utilities that have to figure out how to meet the demand without passing costs straight to ratepayers.
And what does this mean practically for electric bills?
If a big facility comes online without new infrastructure, local taxpayers could see higher rates because the grid has to handle sudden spikes in demand.
Water is another big piece, right?
Exactly. These centers use a lot for cooling, and places like Pittsfield are worried about long-term supply and quality for existing homes and farms.
Farmland is getting pulled into this too.
Yesterday voters in Augusta Township overturned rezoning that would have turned agricultural land into a data center site, keeping it from shifting to industrial use.
That vote blocked the project outright. How are towns balancing the tax revenue these projects promise against those land-use concerns?
Residents are saying the noise, traffic and infrastructure strain outweigh the benefits, especially when it changes the character of rural areas near Ann Arbor.
Pittsfield's rules could become a template. What happens next there?
The changes would affect future projects and could influence other Washtenaw County townships that are watching closely.
Are there signs this local pushback is moving beyond town halls?
Yesterday a candidate who campaigned against data center growth won a Democratic primary for state House, shifting the fight into the legislature for that district.
And we saw something similar at the congressional level.
Will Lawrence defeated Haley Stevens in the MI-7 Democratic primary after vowing to block data centers, moving the debate over power demand and tax breaks into Congress.
Voters in Washtenaw and surrounding counties now have a representative who made this central to the race.
At the same time, Washtenaw voters killed a $1 billion rezoning in a rural township that would have allowed heavy power and water use.
That's a direct block on large-scale development. How are people 30 miles away supposed to think about this?
They have a stake because grid costs and water decisions don't stop at township lines.
Western Michigan had its own vote yesterday.
Residents in a Holland-area township rejected a proposed data center at the ballot box, ending months of debate over noise, power and property values.
That shows opposition can win even after site plans advance.
Nearby communities are now looking at it as a precedent.
In Ingham County, Mason voters narrowed their council field in a race shaped by a proposed data center.
Eight candidates remain after the primary, and November winners will decide whether the plan moves forward amid concerns over electricity rates and zoning.
Another township took a different route yesterday.
Independence Township supervisors approved a moratorium that stops new proposals while rules are written, giving Oakland County residents time to decide on power, water and land use.
That pause could become a model for slowing builds elsewhere.
Overall it feels like communities are testing how much control they can keep over these projects.
What are the stakes if more townships follow Pittsfield's lead?
Developers might face longer timelines or stricter limits, while ratepayers get more say in how costs are shared.
And on the flip side, what if the Monroe lawsuit goes the other way?
It could limit local bans and force more projects through, raising the same grid and water questions for places 30 miles away.
Pittsfield's hearing is today, so this could move quickly.
Residents will have a chance to weigh in directly on the proposed ordinance.
How might this affect the bigger picture of Michigan's data center growth?
It adds momentum to the idea that local rules can shape where and how these facilities get built.
Anything else we should watch in the coming days?
Other Washtenaw townships are already looking at similar zoning tweaks.
The pattern seems clear: voters and officials want more guardrails before these projects scale up.
That brings us to quick hits on the other stories from yesterday.
Let's start with the Monroe Township lawsuit. What's the latest there?
The township is asking a federal judge to dismiss the $300 million suit filed after it banned new data centers, testing whether locals can block big power and water users.
And the primary results?
A data center opponent won a Democratic state House primary, moving the debate into the legislature, while Will Lawrence beat Haley Stevens in MI-7 after campaigning against large projects.
Voter rejections kept coming.
Washtenaw residents killed a $1 billion rezoning, Augusta Township blocked farmland rezoning, and Holland-area voters rejected a project outright.
Mason and Independence added their own chapters.
Mason narrowed its council race in a data center fight, and Independence passed a moratorium to pause new proposals while rules are written.
That covers the wave of pushback. Now let's look at what's on deck today.
Warren City Council has an education session on data centers and water concerns.
Pittsfield Charter Township Planning Commission holds a public hearing on its proposed Data Center Ordinance.
And the Michigan Public Service Commission meets, with potential discussion of utility filings that could touch data center demand.
Listeners can check those agendas directly if they want to attend or weigh in.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Pittsfield Cracks Down on Data Center Sprawl as Local Resistance Spreads
